item.text: {"chapter_id":"1B","answers":[{"question_id":"1B.1","answer":"Mexico’s government consistently articulated risk-reducing nuclear diplomacy: it supported disarmament, nonproliferation, safeguards, de-alerting, and prohibition of nuclear use, including 2023 UN positions and the vote supporting prohibition of nuclear weapons. Mexico also discontinued plans for three new nuclear units while continuing existing-plant safety work. These are favorable formal-policy choices, but most evidence concerns state-level diplomacy or agencies rather than a personally documented López Obrador decision, and implementation or measurable risk reduction is not established. The administration’s broader energy and security choices created institutional conflicts, resource constraints, and cybersecurity weaknesses that qualify the favorable record. The evidence therefore supports declared restraint and some institutional risk reduction, but not a fully attributable or demonstrably consequential presidential program across existential risks.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E003","BATCH-0013-E005","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0040-E002","BATCH-0040-E007","BATCH-0042-E002","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0044-E006","BATCH-0045-E012","BATCH-0045-E013","BATCH-0048-E014"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0017-E006","BATCH-0047-E010","BATCH-0052-E024"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Direct presidential attribution is absent for most nuclear-regulatory and multilateral actions.","Diplomatic positions and treaty status do not prove domestic implementation, funding, or outcomes.","The candidate index provides limited evidence on resource choices specifically made for existential-risk reduction."]},{"question_id":"1B.2","answer":"Mexico’s official rhetoric during and entering 2023 rejected nuclear threats, elevated alert, nuclear use, and reliance on nuclear deterrence, and advocated disarmament, risk reduction, and de-alerting. No evidence in the index shows López Obrador issuing nuclear threats or apocalyptic language, and Mexico’s formal diplomatic posture was generally responsible. However, absence of documented reckless rhetoric is not proof of restraint, and the index contains little evidence about operational doctrine, orders, alert status, or military posture. The conclusion is therefore favorable at the diplomatic-rhetoric level but qualified by weak evidence on operational corroboration and direct presidential authorship.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0042-E002","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0044-E006","BATCH-0045-E013","BATCH-0048-E014","BATCH-0013-E005"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0042-E002","BATCH-0043-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The evidence is primarily diplomatic statements, not operational doctrine or orders.","No source directly documents López Obrador’s personal wording or control of nuclear-related military posture.","Silence in the candidate index cannot establish that reckless rhetoric never occurred."]},{"question_id":"1B.3","answer":"Mexico had substantial nuclear-safety institutions, including CNSNS inspection and sanction powers, CFE safety systems, monitoring, corrective-action processes, training, emergency exercises, spent-fuel planning, and post-Fukushima mitigation. Funding and staffing were documented, and some incidents were investigated without reported public or worker radiological harm. The record is mixed: CNSNS lacked full legal-administrative independence, staffing and knowledge-management gaps persisted, human-factors inspections were absent during 2019–2021, sanctions remained pending, temporary waste capacity was constrained, and 2023 radiological-source thefts showed degradation of defence in depth. Cybersecurity controls were also materially weak in military institutions, including unpatched systems, inadequate monitoring, and reported austerity-related capacity problems. These safeguards and responses are mainly attributable to CFE, CNSNS, and other agencies rather than personally to López Obrador; implementation was real but incomplete and outcomes only partly verified.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0002-E005","BATCH-0002-E007","BATCH-0002-E008","BATCH-0002-E010","BATCH-0002-E011","BATCH-0002-E012","BATCH-0031-E001","BATCH-0031-E002","BATCH-0040-E011"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E002","BATCH-0002-E006","BATCH-0002-E009","BATCH-0002-E013","BATCH-0038-E002","BATCH-0047-E010","BATCH-0011-E005","BATCH-0008-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not establish presidential direction, budget adequacy, or complete closure of corrective actions.","Government-reported safety completion and incident responses receive limited independent verification.","Nuclear command-and-control evidence concerns civilian nuclear safety more than nuclear weapons custody or launch authority."]},{"question_id":"1B.4","answer":"Mexico’s formal posture was strongly supportive of arms control, nonproliferation, disarmament, IAEA safeguards, the NPT, the Additional Protocol, the TPNW, the CTBT, verification, inspections, and risk reduction. During 2023 it presided over the TPNW meeting, co-sponsored relevant resolutions, voted for a resolution prohibiting nuclear use, supported regional disarmament training, and participated in 1540 implementation and biosafety peer-review mechanisms. These actions show diplomatic support and institutional engagement. They do not, however, establish that López Obrador personally directed them, that Mexico added domestic resources, or that treaty obligations were newly implemented or enforced during 2023. The evidence supports good-faith formal compliance and advocacy, with substantial implementation uncertainty.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E005","BATCH-0020-E001","BATCH-0020-E004","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0031-E001","BATCH-0031-E002","BATCH-0040-E002","BATCH-0040-E007","BATCH-0042-E002","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0044-E001","BATCH-0044-E006","BATCH-0045-E013"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E003","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0053-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Treaty signature, votes, sponsorship, and conference participation do not prove domestic implementation or compliance enforcement.","No evidence establishes Mexico’s funding, inspection record, or response to specific treaty violations during 2023.","Most actions are state or ministry actions without direct presidential attribution."]},{"question_id":"1B.5","answer":"The candidate index contains no evidence that López Obrador formally or operationally used nuclear capability to authorize, shield, or intensify conventional aggression, territorial coercion, or domestic repression. Mexico had no demonstrated nuclear-warfighting posture in the supplied evidence, and its diplomatic statements opposed nuclear threats and emphasized peaceful dispute resolution. The conclusion is qualified because the record does not provide a systematic assessment of military doctrine, conventional coercion, or whether other forms of state power were used repressively under nuclear or strategic cover. The available evidence supports no demonstrated nuclear shielding, not affirmative proof that all coercive conduct was absent.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0042-E002","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0045-E012","BATCH-0048-E014","BATCH-0044-E001"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E006","BATCH-0018-E003","BATCH-0018-E013","BATCH-0026-E013","BATCH-0026-E020"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No source directly examines nuclear or strategic coercive shielding of Mexican conventional operations.","Evidence of surveillance and institutional repression is not evidence of nuclear-enabled repression.","The index does not establish a complete presidential military-doctrine record."]},{"question_id":"1B.6","answer":"Mexico demonstrated formal and multilateral engagement with proliferation controls: it endorsed export controls and safeguards, chaired regional illicit-arms and trafficking mechanisms, participated in 1540 peer review, updated its assistance request, supported biological-material controls, and joined efforts to strengthen biosafety and biosecurity. A 2023 UN report also records port container-control and anti-smuggling initiatives, although attribution is institutional rather than personal. The record does not show a documented case in which López Obrador or his government exposed and corrected proliferation assistance or evasion by an ally, proxy, client, firm, or domestic faction. Arms-transfer reporting compliance and domestic enforcement remain unclear, so the evidence supports formal engagement but only limited proof of effective control.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0015-E016","BATCH-0020-E003","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0042-E002","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0045-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E003","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0053-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No concrete domestic licensing, interdiction, prosecution, or corrective-action case is supplied.","The sources do not establish the substance or implementation of Mexico’s 1540 assistance request.","Formal participation and institutional initiatives are not equivalent to effective enforcement."]},{"question_id":"1B.7","answer":"Mexico’s nuclear institutions employed technical personnel, safety-culture programs, peer reviews, monitoring, training, and regional scientific cooperation, and Mexico supported transparent IAEA review and biosafety-related expert mechanisms. These are favorable signs of reliance on technical expertise. Conversely, CNSNS lacked full legal-administrative independence, knowledge-management and staffing gaps persisted, CIDE reported suspension of external research administration and researcher commissions in 2023, and military cybersecurity weaknesses were associated with insufficient specialist capacity. Surveillance allegations, official denials, and pressure on independent institutions further qualify the environment for dissent and independent expertise. Most nuclear appointments and staffing decisions are not personally attributable to López Obrador, so the evidence supports partial institutional expertise with meaningful independence and resourcing weaknesses.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E002","BATCH-0002-E006","BATCH-0002-E007","BATCH-0002-E008","BATCH-0031-E001","BATCH-0031-E002","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0053-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0019-E006","BATCH-0047-E010","BATCH-0018-E003","BATCH-0018-E013","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0053-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not provide a complete roster or quality assessment of presidential appointments.","CIDE funding disruption may reflect administrative delay; causal responsibility is not fully identified.","Allegations concerning surveillance and dissent are not finally adjudicated for every incident."]},{"question_id":"1B.8","answer":"The available evidence shows some operational crisis safeguards: Laguna Verde emergency exercises identified improvements in command-and-control, training, shelters, hospitals, and public information; corrective-action systems, drills, and quarterly regulatory meetings were used after safety events. Mexico also advocated preventive diplomacy, mediation, and confidence-building regarding the Russia–Ukraine war. The record is mixed because exercises produced 78 findings, follow-up was delayed, specialized mitigation remained incomplete, nuclear-safety incidents and radiological thefts occurred, and military cyber breaches were followed by secrecy or limited publicly documented correction. These events are attributable mainly to agencies, while the index directly attributes diplomatic proposals to López Obrador’s government but not their implementation or success. Crisis safeguards existed, but correction and transparency were incomplete.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0002-E007","BATCH-0002-E010","BATCH-0002-E011","BATCH-0002-E012","BATCH-0045-E012","BATCH-0008-E006","BATCH-0040-E011"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E010","BATCH-0002-E011","BATCH-0038-E002","BATCH-0047-E010","BATCH-0018-E013","BATCH-0011-E005"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not establish whether all exercise findings were closed or whether procedures were materially changed.","The diplomatic initiative’s implementation and effects are not documented.","Cyber and radiological incident responses are incompletely reported and often not personally attributable to López Obrador."]},{"question_id":"1B.9","answer":"Mexico maintained inherited climate, biosecurity, financial-cyber, and nuclear-safety frameworks and in 2023 established a scientific technical committee on GMO biosafety, participated in 1540 and biosafety cooperation, and issued diplomatic warnings about synthetic biology, biotechnology, biogenetics, and emerging dual-use risks. It also supported international controls and scientific review. The adverse record includes major military cyber breaches, obsolete and unpatched systems, weak monitoring and risk assessment, surveillance-related safeguards and accountability concerns, weakened data-protection institutions, and a proposed cybersecurity bill with broad takedown and criminalization risks. The candidate index supplies little evidence of AI governance and limited proof of funded, enforced, transparently reviewed domestic safeguards for biological or cyber catastrophic risks. Overall, formal recognition and some institutions coexisted with material implementation and accountability gaps.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0039-E002","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0052-E024","BATCH-0027-R01-E009","BATCH-0017-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0008-E006","BATCH-0011-E005","BATCH-0014-E006","BATCH-0018-E003","BATCH-0018-E013","BATCH-0026-E013","BATCH-0026-E015","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0026-E021","BATCH-0047-E010","BATCH-0053-E001","BATCH-0053-E002","BATCH-0053-E003","BATCH-0053-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No meaningful AI-specific policy evidence is supplied.","Later biosecurity indicators cannot be treated as direct 2023 measurements.","Cybersecurity and surveillance evidence often concerns institutions under the administration without proving López Obrador’s personal authorization or knowledge.","Policy proposals and diplomatic statements do not establish implementation, funding, or effectiveness."]},{"question_id":"1B.10","answer":"By the end of 2023, Mexico retained a generally restrained diplomatic nuclear posture, a TPNW commitment, established nuclear-safety institutions, ongoing corrective-action systems, and participation in disarmament, nonproliferation, biosafety, and 1540 mechanisms. These provide evidence of continuity and some risk-reducing capacity. The end posture was not demonstrably safer across all catastrophic-risk domains: CNSNS remained less than fully independent, nuclear inspection and waste-capacity gaps persisted, radiological-source thefts occurred in 2023, emergency follow-up and specialized mitigation were incomplete, military cybersecurity weaknesses were exposed without fully documented remediation, and privacy, surveillance, and institutional-accountability safeguards deteriorated or remained contested. Much of the favorable posture was inherited or agency-led, while direct presidential attribution and causal evidence of durable improvement are limited. The evidence therefore supports a mixed end-state: responsible nuclear diplomacy and partial safety continuity alongside unresolved or worsened cyber, institutional, and dual-use-risk exposure.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E003","BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0002-E007","BATCH-0002-E011","BATCH-0031-E001","BATCH-0031-E002","BATCH-0042-E002","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0044-E001","BATCH-0044-E006","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E002","BATCH-0002-E009","BATCH-0002-E010","BATCH-0002-E013","BATCH-0038-E002","BATCH-0040-E011","BATCH-0047-E010","BATCH-0011-E005","BATCH-0014-E006","BATCH-0018-E013","BATCH-0026-E020","BATCH-0017-E006","BATCH-0053-E003","BATCH-0053-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is no comprehensive, independent before-and-after existential-risk assessment for 2018–2023.","Many favorable nuclear arrangements predate or are not personally attributable to López Obrador.","Some later indicators are retrospective and cannot establish exact 2023 conditions.","The index provides limited evidence on long-term outcomes, AI risk, and durability of corrective measures."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["The strongest favorable evidence concerns Mexico’s official nuclear disarmament, nonproliferation, and risk-reduction diplomacy; the weakest link is proof of domestic implementation and direct presidential attribution.","Nuclear-safety institutions were active and funded but remained incompletely independent and exposed to operational incidents, unresolved corrective work, and storage or inspection gaps.","Cybersecurity, surveillance accountability, and independent oversight provide substantial adverse evidence for broader catastrophic-risk governance, although personal causation is often uncertain.","The candidate record supports mixed responsibility across the ruler-period rather than a uniformly favorable or adverse account."]}
